text: Building a report in ServiceNow starts in Report Designer, and it always comes down to the same three decisions, made in order.

First, pick a data source — almost always a table, like incident or change request. Second, pick a report type — the shape the chart will take. Third, pick a group-by field — the field whose distinct values become the slices or bars. A Pie chart of open incidents, grouped by priority, filtered to active records, is the canonical first report every admin builds.

ServiceNow ships several real chart types, and the right one depends on the question. Pie charts show the breakdown of a whole. Bar charts compare categories side by side, like incidents by assignment group. Line charts and Time Series show a trend across calendar time. A List report is just a filtered, sorted set of records with no chart at all. And a Pivot Table cross-tabulates two fields at once — priority down the rows, assignment group across the columns — with a count or sum in every cell.

The group-by field decides what the data splits into; the aggregation decides what number shows up for each split. Count is the default — how many records per group. For numeric fields, you can instead sum a value, like total hours logged, or average it, like average time-to-resolve per assignment group — exactly the report a Service Desk Manager would ask for to see which team is falling behind.

Reports use the exact same condition builder from Chapter 5 to filter down to the records that matter — Active is true, for instance, so closed incidents don't dilute the chart. And once a report exists, it doesn't have to be opened by hand. Scheduling it sends the chart by email, daily, weekly, or on a custom recurrence, to any list of users or groups, with no login required.
Table, type, group-by, aggregation, and filter — that's a complete report. Next, Performance Analytics: what a point-in-time report can't show you, and how ServiceNow tracks change over time instead.
